title: The Potion He Cannot Brew
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 34 of 40
content:
There are potions for sleep.

Potions for pain.

Potions for fever, memory, luck, love's imitation, truth, strength, weakness, and the temporary rearrangement of nearly every inconvenient thing a human body can do.

There is no potion for regret.

Snape hated this fact.

I discovered that when he nearly poisoned himself trying to create one.

Not intentionally.

That distinction matters.

The accident began with a commission from St Mungo's for a draught to reduce intrusive memory after curse trauma. Nothing that erased memory. Nothing that suppressed judgment. A therapeutic potion meant to take the sharpest edge off involuntary recollection so patients could sleep.

Snape became obsessed.

At first, productively.

He researched old Calming Draughts, Dreamless Sleep, and experimental treatments from the first war. He rejected anything addictive, anything that dulled cognition too heavily, anything that interfered with Occlumency.

Then he stopped sleeping.

I noticed on day three.

He denied it.

I noticed on day four.

He called me intrusive.

On day five, I found him in the laboratory at four in the morning with three cauldrons running and his left hand shaking badly enough to spill powdered moonstone.

I turned off the nearest flame.

He swore.

“Go to bed.”

“Turn it back on.”

“No.”

“The timing—”

“Is ruined. Good.”

His face went white with anger.

“That batch required six hours.”

“You require sleep.”

“I require results.”

“For St Mungo's?”

“Yes.”

“Only?”

Silence.

There it was.

I looked at the three cauldrons.

“You're trying to brew it for yourself.”

His expression closed.

“No.”

“Severus.”

He flinched at the name.

Not because he disliked it.

Because I used it when I needed him present.

“You want something that will make the memories stop hurting.”

“I want a functional treatment.”

“For yourself.”

His jaw tightened.

“Among others.”

I softened.

“That isn't wrong.”

He looked at me sharply.

“I didn't say it was.”

“You're acting like wanting relief is a moral failure.”

His hand reached for the ingredient tray.

I moved it away.

“Enough.”

“Do not touch my work.”

“Then stop using your work to hurt yourself.”

His eyes went cold.

“I am not hurting myself.”

“You are exhausted, shaking, and brewing three experimental neuroactive potions alone.”

“I know what I am doing.”

“So did you at sixteen when you invented Sectumsempra.”

The words hit like a slap.

Snape recoiled.

I regretted them instantly.

Not the concern.

The weapon.

I had used his past to win.

Exactly what he had once done to me.

“I'm sorry,” I said immediately.

His face was blank.

“That was cruel.”

“Yes.”

“I was scared and I reached for something that would hurt enough to stop you.”

“Yes.”

“I hate that I did it.”

He looked away.

The nearest cauldron bubbled.

I extinguished it too.

This time he did not stop me.

“I am still asking you to stop,” I said.

His shoulders lowered.

“Fine.”

Not agreement.

Surrender from exhaustion.

I took the stirring rod from his hand.

His fingers were cold.

“Sit.”

“You are enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

He sat.

I brought water.

He drank because he was too tired to argue well.

Then his face changed.

“What?” I asked.

Snape looked at the cauldron behind me.

The experimental mixture had turned from blue to clear.

“That should not happen.”

I turned.

A thin vapor curled upward.

Sweet.

Too sweet.

“Don't breathe—”

Too late.

The room tilted.

Snape moved faster than I had seen him move in months.

He shoved me toward the door and cast a shield over the cauldrons.

My knees failed.

He caught me.

The irony would have been funny under different circumstances.

“Stay awake.”

His voice came from far away.

“What was that?”

“Concentrated dream suppressant. The stabilizer inverted.”

“That sounds bad.”

“It is bad.”

“Excellent.”

My mouth felt numb.

Snape half-carried me into the corridor.

“Help!” he shouted.

I had never heard him shout for help.

The sound scared me more than the potion.

Madam Pomfrey arrived with McGonagall minutes later.

I remember pieces.

A bitter antidote.

Snape's hand gripping mine.

Pomfrey ordering him out.

Snape refusing.

My own voice saying his name because I could not think of anything else.

Then sleep.

When I woke in the hospital wing, afternoon light filled the windows.

Snape sat beside the bed.

He looked terrible.

“You look terrible,” I said.

His eyes closed.

“Good. You are still tactless.”

“You're welcome.”

He took my hand.

His grip was too tight.

“I'm okay?”

“Yes.”

“Any damage?”

“No.”

“You?”

“I was shielded by position.”

“Convenient.”

His mouth did not move.

I realized he had been crying.

Not currently.

But recently enough that the skin beneath his eyes was red.

My chest hurt.

“Severus.”

“No.”

“What?”

“Do not comfort me for nearly killing you.”

“You didn't.”

“My potion did.”

“An experimental accident—”

“Caused by exhaustion I refused to acknowledge.”

His voice broke slightly.

I did not argue.

He needed responsibility, not denial.

“Yes,” I said.

His face tightened.

“You were reckless.”

“Yes.”

“You scared me.”

His eyes closed.

“Yes.”

“I am angry.”

“You should be.”

“And I love you.”

His eyes opened.

“That is not absolution.”

“I know.”

“It is not permission to do it again.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

I squeezed his hand.

“Now you can comfort me.”

His expression crumpled by a fraction.

He lifted my fingers to his mouth and kissed them.

“I am sorry,” he said.

“I know.”

Later, Pomfrey banned both of us from the laboratory for three days.

Snape objected.

I did not.

He looked betrayed.

The potion project went on hold for a month.

When we returned to it, we worked only in daylight, only one experimental cauldron at a time, with a third reviewer from St Mungo's present.

The final formula did not erase regret.

It did not erase nightmares.

It simply made sleep easier for some patients without stealing the memories that belonged to them.

Snape called the result limited.

I called it humane.

He eventually agreed.

There are potions for many things.

There are no potions that make the past stop being true.

Maybe that was mercy too.
